title: Tent at noon; second day — the firmament
english: …economy from a clear example: that unquenchable light surrounds the outer place of heaven, while mist held the inside before the light was made. As if someone at steady noon pitched a tent of dense matter and made improvised darkness — and the enclosed place cannot be lit at all unless a gleam of light flashes out — so such unsubstantial darkness held the world covered under heaven, which God parted by creating the light, naming it day and the darkness night. For when light is poured out, day comes; when it is drawn in, night answers. That is why in measuring times we count days, not nights. On the second day God made the firmament. This is other than the heaven made from the beginning. Some have said it is the same — a working-out of the second, they say, because there the making of earth and heaven was given in summary, and here Scripture hands over more carefully how it came to be. We say they are other and other: for another name and a distinct use of the second heaven are handed down. So this one is other than the one made in the beginning, of a firmer nature. And God parted the water that was under the firmament. For he divided the boundless nature of the waters so that some would be above the firmament and some below. Ether is fiery and burning, and would have consumed the whole mainland if it were not held by the Maker’s bound. That is why there is also aerial water carried up in clouds from the rise of vapors — which rivers, springs, lakes, and all the seas send forth — so that ether may not burn everything up. It happens thus: […] the exhalations gather toward the height, air is packed by the press of winds, and the moistures sown in the cloud, drawing near one another, become drops and by the weight of what has been gathered are sent downward. Snow forms from the waters this way: the wet, struck back by the violence of the winds, foams up; struck through and through and chilled, it freezes, and when the cloud is shattered the snow is carried down. Thunder […] is a rebound — driven in the hollows of the clouds and bursting out by force, it makes the sound of thunder.

title: Third day — dry land, seas, and plants
english: On the third day, by God’s command, the water was gathered into its gatherings and the dry appeared; and he called the dry earth, and the systems of the waters he called seas. It was gathered into one gathering so that it might not […] from the places where it is and, spilling over, cover the mainland. That is why the sea, often raging from winds and rising to a great height in waves, when it only touches the shores dissolves its rush into foam and turns back — bridled by sand, weakest of all things. What kept the Red Sea from flooding all Egypt, which lies lower than it, and joining the neighboring deep, if it were not bound by the Maker’s command? That this is true Sesostris the Egyptian and Darius the Mede persuaded us in deed: attempting to join the Egyptian and Indian seas, they could not. So much lower than the Red Sea is Egypt. He ordered the waters gathered into one gathering, and that another sea not arise from this one, but remain in the first collection. For there were many […] waters […] hollows […] gathering and ravines. And “the systems of the waters he called seas” points to the gulfs left in their own shape by the surrounding land — northern sea, southern sea, eastern and western deeps, and their proper names: Pontus, Aegean, Ionian, Sardinian, Sicilian, Tyrrhenian. Not chance pools of water ended in one sea or system, but the greatest and outstanding; one must not think also of marsh and lake. As fire, even when crumbled small, is still poured as one under the air, so with water: though there are small divided systems, there is one gathering that separates the whole element from the rest. For the sea’s water is the spring of all moisture about the earth, and the whole earth is under-channeled, and it is distributed through unseen passages, as some underground places of the mainland show. The flowing sea, running through narrow places, when left in crooked and upright exits, pushed by the force of the wind breaks the earth’s surface and, coming outside, becomes drinkable, changed to sweetness by filtering. Again, when left in hot places toward the exit, drawn by the same cause under the wind it comes boiling. This too is the spring of the aerial waters: its waters drawn up through clouds, warmed by the sun’s ray, chilled in the cloud’s shade, and clarified from that height, grow sweet and sprinkle the mainland. On the same day God also ordered the earth to sprout pasture of grass, sowing seed according to kind, and fruit-tree making fruit whose seed is in it. And still now the order of what grows witnesses to the first arranging. Sprouting leads every herb and every plant: when the earth has moisture in measure and warmth, the seed is cast into it and becomes soft and many-seeded, and beginning from the earth about it draws to itself what is its own and kindred, and fattened it spreads — so that it roots downward and pushes upward, and puts out stalks equal in number to the roots. As the sprout is always warmed, the moisture drawn through the roots is carried along by the earth’s heat with the nourishment, and this is portioned into stalk and husk and the wheat’s cases and the wheat itself and the awns. The wheat’s stalk is girded with joints so that, like some bonds, they may bear the weight of the ears. The stalk is also hollow so that it may be a case for the grain, not easy plunder for seed-pickers. It has thrust out the awns like spears to keep off the harms of small creatures. Oats stand empty through and through because they are not weighted at the head. And if harmful plants sprouted with the nourishing — hellebore, aconite, mandrake, and the juice of the poppy — none of these was taken idle for use. Starlings feed on hemlock by the making of their body: having fine passages to the heart, they manage to send off what is swallowed; quails eat hellebore and take no harm, having a peculiar temperament. By mandrake physicians bring on sleep, and with opium they lay fierce pains to rest. With hemlock they wither mad appetites, and with hellebore they soothe chronic sufferings. “And fruit-tree making fruit.” And all sprang from the earth in one turn of time that were not before, each with its own property, each known by its own character. Olive, date-palm, and cypress grow tall. And of these some are not many-branched — fir and cypress, and sometimes the palm. Evergreen are olive, palm, laurel, myrtle, pine, cypress, fir, juniper, thuja, and what Arcadians call philodrys; also phyleos, cedar, pine, box, holm-oak, arake, lathyrus. The rose then sprouted without the thorn; later the thorn was yoked to the flower’s beauty — so that having grief set beside delight we may remember the sin through which the earth was condemned to sprout thorns and thistles for us. The almond blossoms first and brings fruit last. The bitter almond, its stem bored toward the root and receiving a pitched pine wedge driven into the middle pith, turns the harsh juices to edible sweetness. The sharp pomegranate, receiving the same treatment, turns to sweetness. The female palm lets down her branches as if longing for the male’s embrace; and farmers, putting the male’s pollen into her branches, set her back into her proper upright shape. The mulberry sprouts late but does not lag the others in fruiting. Olive, linden, white poplar, and elm turn their leaves upside-down after the summer solstice; and by this all know that the summer turns have come.

title: Figs and vines; fourth day — sun and moon
english: Farmers keep the cultivated fig’s fruit from falling thus: stripping the wild fig’s early figs, they arrange that it remain unfallen. For the tiniest creature inside the wild fig, settling at the base of the cultivated fig, fences off the outer breeze so the fig may not grow unpleasant and drop. Since the fig’s fruit is soft, it is covered with thick leaves; the walnut, being hard, is sheltered by a light cast of leaves. That is why the vine’s leaf is split — so the cluster may both turn aside harms from the air and take in the sun’s ray through the sparseness. So nothing is idle; God arranged all by unspeakable wisdom. For one water, carried or drawn through the root, nourishes the stem one way, the pith another, the bark another, the wood another, the root itself another; and from the same moisture wine is constituted in the vine, oil in the olive, and something else in another. And even among sweet fruits the difference of richness is unspeakable: one sweetness in the vine, another in the apple, another in fig and date-palm. And the trees’ tears themselves differ: one is the tear of the mastic, another the juice of balsam — finest of all myrrhs, and it abounds when it grows at Jericho. When locals cut it from the bushes with a sharp stone, juice wells up. Some also say amber is the juice of plants, fixed into stone nature. 4. On the fourth day God created the two great lights — sun and moon — in the firmament of heaven, for lighting upon the earth, to part between the day and the night. This solar light was prepared as a vehicle for that first-born light. As fire is one thing and the lamp another — the one has the power to light, the other the power to show light to those who need it — and as whiteness is one thing and the whitened body another, so these too, different in nature, are joined by the Maker’s power. And let no one think day and sun are the same. First the Maker prepared simple light, which he also called day; then the sun composed of fire and light. As we see the earth has fire wrought in its own breast, so also the sun has light: for light coming together with fire made the most radiant sun. But someone may object: How is this clear when the division is not seen? For light is not seen by itself and fire by itself. Let such a one know how many things fire puts forward in itself — gleam, heat, yellowness — which the all-wise craftsman, portioning out, hints at their composition. When he wants to warm the living thing, he takes the fire’s heat: it has the heat but not the light. But the warmth was parted in the living thing from the brightness; again he takes the yellow. And we see the yellow, but no longer the hot and shining. And again he portions off the warmth and gives only the gleam — as one may see in lightning, which flashing only lights and does not also warm. The same example holds for the moon. For she, lit by the sun, becomes more apparent, as the sun by the day. The moon’s form is coal-like, as one may see in eclipse: when the sun lifts its own brightness from her, it makes her dim; lighting her, it makes her full-shining. For somehow putting on the solar light she becomes brighter; in the same way the sun, putting on the day’s light, is more brilliant — that day neither being fire nor again warming, but only lighting. That the sun is composed of fire is clear from its burning and blazing. “To part between the day and the night”: he set the sun to the measures of the day and the moon to those of the night. Night is the earth’s shadow when the sun is hidden. As in the day, when something stands in the way, shadow comes and light is set beside it, so night is constituted when the air about the earth is shadowed. And the sun, which from the beginning received light from the Maker, has this always hidden in itself; the moon is not so, but continually puts it off…
